128.title: Jesus’ Early Manhood
128.b0.ask: “Why did the Creator Son live as an ordinary carpenter without using his powers, and slowly prepare to leave his family?”
128.b2.p: In Paper 127 Jesus passed through an adolescence full of trials and became a man of twenty. Paper 128 covers his early manhood, from twenty-one to twenty-six. He came into the world like other children; he did not choose his parents, and he grew up wrestling with the ups and downs of his surroundings just as every other mortal of this world does.
128.b3.p: The paper asks us always to remember that Michael’s bestowal on Urantia had two purposes. Every other benefit was secondary to these two.
128.b4.q: “⟦Q 128:7.2⟧Regardless of who I am and what power I may or may not wield, I always have been, and always will be, subject to the will of my Paradise Father.⟦/Q⟧”
128.b7.t: To live a perfect life in mortal flesh and so complete his sovereignty of Nebadon
To reveal the Universal Father to mortals and lead them to him
128.b8.p: Now a grown man, fully aware of his twofold nature, Jesus set out in earnest on the task of experiencing the life of the lowest of intelligent creatures. Yet he had already joined his two natures into one — Jesus of Nazareth. He labored, grew weary, slept, and was hungry, and he experienced the whole range of human feeling.
128.b9.p: Until his baptism he used no supernatural powers, and he emptied himself of the attributes of his prehuman existence. He was truly a man among men. His self-realization of divinity was a slow and natural evolutionary revelation. It began in Jerusalem when he was about thirteen and was completed at his baptism in the Jordan, and nothing supernatural happened in between.
128.b10.q: ⟦Q 128:1.5⟧We have a Sovereign who was in all points tested and tempted like as we are, yet without sin.⟦/Q⟧
128.b11.p: Later, when he was called by many titles, he did not object. Only once, when he was called Immanuel, did he reply, “⟦Q 128:1.11⟧Not I, that is my elder brother.⟦/Q⟧” This year he took his brother Joseph up to the Passover, and when asked about his mission he answered only, “⟦Q 128:1.15|128:5.4|128:7.5⟧My hour has not yet come.⟦/Q⟧”
128.b13.p: While his brothers and sisters went through the trials of adolescence, Jesus helped them adjust. A family council decided to spread the family’s trades, and Simon began to work as a mason. Late in the year Jesus worked for six months under a smith in Sepphoris and learned the craft of working metal.
128.b14.p: Before leaving, he formally appointed James, then eighteen, as acting head of the family, and had every member of the family promise to obey James. He could have come home every night, but he chose to stay away; his real motive was to train James and Joseph to carry the family’s responsibilities. He never again took the reins back from James. In Sepphoris he worked alongside gentiles and eagerly studied their way of life and their minds.
128.b15.t: James appointed acting head of the family; financial responsibility handed over
Joseph entrusted with the family funds and their management
Joseph made head of the family, and James “head of my father’s house”
128.b17.p: With four of them now working, the family was a little better off, and Jesus took three weeks away from work to go up to the Passover with Simon. Going up through the Decapolis and returning by the coast road, he came to know northern Palestine well. On the way a wealthy merchant of Damascus invited him to join in his business of importing goods from the Orient, but he declined, saying he could not go far from his family.
128.b18.p: In Jerusalem he talked for four hours with Stephen, a young Hellenist, about the true God and true worship. Stephen never forgot those words. Later, preaching the gospel boldly, he was stoned and became the first martyr. Saul of Tarsus, who stood by, was so moved by this death that he went on to become Paul.
128.b19.p: Mary was upset to hear that Jesus had been spending time with strangers, especially people from distant lands. The family could not understand his urge to know how people lived and thought, and Mary was slowly giving up her ideas about his divine mission.
128.b21.p: Jesus spent the last four months of this year in Damascus as the merchant’s guest. The merchant wanted to found a school of religious philosophy that would surpass Alexandria, with Jesus at its head, and twelve merchants and bankers promised their support. The paper says this was one of the greatest temptations he faced in his purely human life.
128.b22.p: Jesus helped with the plans for the school, but he would not take charge of it. He knew that his mission must not be supported by an institution of learning, nor directed by a “⟦Q 74:3.5⟧council of men.⟦/Q⟧” He deliberately kept the different episodes of his life apart, so that people would not come to revere the teacher instead of obeying the truths he taught.
128.b23.q: ⟦Q 128:4.7⟧He did not want men to believe in him unless their hearts were responsive to the spiritual realities revealed in his teachings.⟦/Q⟧
128.b25.p: This was the first year in which Jesus was fairly free of family responsibility. In June, at Caesarea, five leading Jews of Alexandria begged him to come to them as a religious teacher. They warned that rebellion in Palestine would be national suicide and that the temple would be destroyed. Jesus declined, saying, “⟦Q 128:1.15|128:5.4|128:7.5⟧My hour has not yet come,⟦/Q⟧” and he would not accept even the purse they offered him.
128.b26.q: “⟦Q 128:5.4⟧The house of Joseph has never received alms, and we cannot eat another's bread as long as I have strong arms and my brothers can labor.⟦/Q⟧”
128.b27.t: He could not go far from his family
The Damascus school of religious philosophy
He could not be bound by a council of men
The call to teach in Alexandria
The house of Joseph never received alms
128.b28.p: The remaining six months were the quietest period of his life. He enjoyed deep communion with his heavenly Father and made great progress in mastering the human mind. In December James asked to marry Esta, and Jacob the mason asked to marry Miriam. Jesus gave his consent, on condition that they be ready to carry on the household.
128.b30.p: Jesus was one of the most robust and refined specimens of manhood since the days of Adam, and his spirit was truly humanly divine. In this year, with all the debts paid, he went with his youngest brother, Jude, on Jude’s first visit to the temple. But Jude protested hotly to a Roman guard who had spoken rudely to a Jewish girl, and he was arrested. Jesus stayed with his brother in prison for two days.
128.b31.p: Before the magistrate Jesus carefully explained what had happened and won his brother’s release. He told the family nothing, but three weeks later he had a long talk with Jude. Jude never forgot the patience and tolerance of his brother-father. This was the last Passover Jesus kept with his family. Children always crowded around his repair shop, begging “Uncle Joshua” for stories, and he could pass perfectly from a profound discussion to the play of children.
128.b33.p: This year Jesus became strongly aware that he had vast potential powers, but he was convinced that, as the Son of Man, he must not use them until his hour had come. When his brothers wanted to throw Jude out, he counseled patience: persuade him by the way you live, so that he will choose the better way for himself. The paper says again that his main mission was to gain creature experience and so achieve the sovereignty of Nebadon — and that in doing this he gave the supreme revelation of the Father.
128.b34.p: Jude settled down as a fisherman at Magdala, and in November there was a double wedding: James and Esta, and Miriam and Jacob. The next day Jesus told James privately that he was preparing to leave home. He handed over the repair shop and made James “⟦Q 128:7.13⟧head and protector of my father’s house.⟦/Q⟧” He promised to keep sending something each month until his hour came. So he finished preparing to enter the second stage of his adult life, apart from his home.
128.b36.p: Paper 128 shows six years in which the Creator of a universe held great powers but did not use them, living as an ordinary carpenter and head of a family. Again and again he declined the honor of heading a school and offers of generous support, and he carefully kept the episodes of his life apart so that people would not exalt the teacher above the truth. At the same time he trained his brothers, one by one, to head the family, so that it could stand without him. His resolve — to remain subject to the Father’s will, whatever powers he held — was the center of this quiet preparation for his public ministry.
128.b37.t: The Creator Son used no powers and lived as a true man among men
He made James acting head of the family and began its independence
He mixed with people of distant lands and planted a seed in Stephen’s heart
He declined to head a school and kept the teacher from being exalted above the truth
He refused Alexandria’s call and gift, and enjoyed deep communion with the Father
He stood by his arrested brother and became the children’s uncle
He made James head of his father’s house and finished preparing to leave
128.b39.box: Whatever powers he held, Jesus always remained subject to the Father’s will, and in an ordinary life he quietly prepared for his public ministry.
129.title: The Later Adult Life of Jesus
129.b0.ask: “Why did Jesus, once he had left home, live as a boatbuilder and a traveler — and how did he complete his mortal life before he was thirty?”
129.b2.p: In Paper 128 Jesus made James the head of his father’s house and finished his preparations for leaving home. Paper 129 covers the three years after he had fully and finally separated himself from the management of the Nazareth family. Right up to his baptism he kept contributing to the family finances, and he never stopped caring about the spiritual welfare of his brothers and sisters and the happiness of his widowed mother.
129.b3.p: Leaving was not easy. The paper tells us that the more fully we give ourselves to our fellows, the more we come to love them — and since Jesus had given himself so fully to his family, he loved them with a great and fervent affection. For more than four years the family had slowly sensed that he was preparing to go, and this gradual awakening softened the sadness of the parting.
129.b4.p: Where, then, did Jesus go after he left home, what did he do there, and what did those years mean for his bestowal?
129.b5.q: ⟦Q 129:4.7⟧Jesus is the new and living way from man to God, from the partial to the perfect, from the earthly to the heavenly, from time to eternity.⟦/Q⟧
129.b8.p: On a rainy Sunday morning in January of A.D. 21, Jesus took unceremonious leave of his family. He said only that he was going to visit the cities around the Sea of Galilee. He never again was a regular member of that household. At Capernaum he called on his father’s friend Zebedee, a boatbuilder, who invited him to join in making improved boats. Together they created a new style of boat, far safer on the lake, and greatly improved the method of steaming the boards. In less than five years practically every craft on the lake had been built in Zebedee’s shop.
129.b9.p: Jesus lived in Zebedee’s home and greatly enjoyed working with a father-partner after so many years of working alone. When taxes came due, he registered himself as a “⟦Q 129:1.8⟧skilled craftsman of Capernaum,⟦/Q⟧” and from then on he was known as a resident of Capernaum. He led the services in the new synagogue more than half the time that year, studied there at least five evenings a week, and got along wonderfully with young people. His secret was simple: he was always interested in what they were doing, and he seldom offered advice unless they asked for it.
129.b10.p: Each evening after supper he held a session of questions and answers. He spoke freely about politics, sociology, science, and philosophy, but he never presumed to speak with authoritative finality except about religion — the relation of man to God. It was among Zebedee’s workers that he was first called “the Master.” This year he attained new and high levels of conscious contact with his indwelling Thought Adjuster, and it was the last year of his settled life.
129.b11.t: What he valued most in Jesus
Jesus as a teacher and philosopher
129.b13.p: In March of A.D. 22 Jesus left Capernaum, asking John Zebedee to send money to his family each month from the funds owed him. John promised to watch over the family as he would care for his own mother, brothers, and sisters. John and Zebedee then used Jesus’ money to buy a small house in Capernaum and held the title in trust. In this way Jesus became the owner of a house — but no one told him about it.
129.b14.p: In Jerusalem, carrying a letter of introduction from Salome, he was taken by the former high priest Annas to visit the many academies of the religious teachers. He inspected them carefully, yet he never asked a single question in public. Near the end of Passover week he met a wealthy traveler from India and his son, a young man of about seventeen, who were looking for someone to serve as interpreter and as tutor for the son. Jesus hesitated because of his family, so the traveler offered to advance him a year’s wages to protect them from want, and Jesus agreed. He told only Zebedee about the journey, and Zebedee kept the secret for almost two years.
129.b15.p: Meanwhile the family in Nazareth, knowing nothing of the arrangement with John, decided the time had come to manage without Jesus’ help. James remembered his agreement and, with his brothers, took full responsibility for the household. Before Jesus returned, the family had just about given him up as dead; only Zebedee’s assurances kept hope alive in Mary’s heart. Still, the family got along well, and John faithfully brought presents each month to Mary and Ruth, as Jesus had instructed.
129.b17.p: The whole of the twenty-ninth year was spent finishing the tour of the Mediterranean world. On the journey Jesus was known as the Damascus scribe, and on the return trip as the Jewish tutor. He never revealed this journey to his family or to the apostles. His family believed he had been in Alexandria, and when he came home he did nothing to change their minds.
129.b18.p: To understand such apparently strange conduct, the paper asks us to keep the motive of the bestowal in mind. Jesus was careful not to build up an overattractive and attention-consuming personal career. He was dedicated to revealing the heavenly Father to his fellow mortals while living his own life subject to the Father’s will. And he lived this life not for Urantia alone but for his entire universe of Nebadon.
129.b19.t: Those he met and loved on the journey
129.b20.p: The real purpose of the trip was to know men. By its end Jesus virtually knew, with all human certainty, that he was a Creator Son of the Universal Father. Little by little the Adjuster brought up in his mind shadowy memories of his Paradise experience, and the last of these memories became clear on the very day of his baptism in the Jordan.
129.b22.p: To the celestial intelligences who watched, this Mediterranean trip was the most enthralling of all Jesus’ earth experiences. He was still the carpenter, the boatbuilder, and the scribe — still a man among men. His purely human religious experience nearly reached its peak in this twenty-ninth year, and it was completed, as a mortal of the realm, on the day of his baptism.
129.b23.p: He was a child of joy and a being of rare good humor, and yet he was also a “⟦Q 129:4.4⟧man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.⟦/Q⟧” He experienced those higher phases of human and Adjuster reconciliation which so few Urantia mortals ever attain. His contemporaries did not all approve of him, but the life he lived received full and unqualified acceptance by the Universal Father.
129.b24.t: Not a pattern for every person to copy in all its details
An example of the way to live
We may live our own lives in the same way and by the same means
The guide of all Paradise pilgrims
129.b25.q: ⟦Q 129:4.7⟧You may not aspire to live his life, but you can resolve to live your lives even as, and by the same means that, he lived his.⟦/Q⟧
129.b26.p: By the end of his twenty-ninth year Jesus had virtually finished the life required of mortals as sojourners in the flesh. He had come to earth as the fullness of God made manifest to man, and he had now become nearly the perfection of man, awaiting the moment to be made manifest to God. And he did all of this before he was thirty years of age.
129.b28.p: Paper 129 shows us three quiet but decisive years after Jesus left home and before his public ministry. In Capernaum he built better boats and shared his life with young people and workmen. On his Mediterranean journey he came to know and love every kind of person. He carefully hid the traces of his own career so that it would not draw attention away from his mission. In this way he lived the mortal life to the full — and that life became not a pattern for us to imitate, but a living way that leads us to live our own lives in the same spirit.
129.b29.t: He left home, built boats, and reached a higher contact with his Adjuster
He entrusted his family to John and quietly set out on a long journey
He traveled to know men and came to know that he was a Creator Son
His life is not a pattern to copy but a way that teaches us how to live
129.b31.box: Before he was thirty, Jesus lived the mortal life to the full and became the new and living way from man to God.
130.title: On the Way to Rome
130.b0.ask: “On the road to Rome, what did ‘the scribe of Damascus’ give to each person he met?”
130.b2.p: In Paper 129 Jesus agreed to travel the Mediterranean world as interpreter for a traveler from India and as tutor for his son. Paper 130 follows the first part of that journey, from Jerusalem to Rome. Jesus left Jerusalem with Gonod and his son Ganid in April of A.D. 22, and he said good-bye to them in December of the following year at Charax on the Persian Gulf.
130.b3.p: He spent about half of each day teaching Ganid and interpreting for Gonod. The rest of his time he gave to close personal contacts with the people he met. Over this long and intimate association Ganid came to love Jesus deeply. Gonod asked him many times to come back with them to India, but Jesus always declined, explaining that he had to return to his family.
130.b4.p: What, then, did this traveler — known as the scribe of Damascus — teach the strangers he met along the way, and what fruit did those brief meetings bear?
130.b5.q: ⟦Q 130:2.6⟧No man is a stranger to one who knows God.⟦/Q⟧
130.b8.t: Malta, Syracuse, Messina, Naples, Capua, Rome
130.b9.p: At Joppa Jesus met Gadiah, a young Philistine who was a seeker after truth. Gadiah asked whether the big fish really did swallow Jonah. Jesus saw that this story had taught the young man the folly of running away from duty, so he said nothing that would destroy that motive. Instead he told him that we are all Jonahs with lives to live in accordance with the will of God — and that the flight from duty is the sacrifice of truth. Gadiah later heard Peter preach and became a profound believer in Jesus.
130.b10.p: At their last meeting Gadiah asked: if God is good, who creates evil? Jesus answered that God’s goodness is so great and real that it cannot contain the small and unreal things of evil. By giving us the power to choose, the Father created the possibility of evil. But evil does not actually exist until an intelligent creature wills it by choosing wrongly, and it becomes sin when that choice is knowing and deliberate.
130.b11.t: Arises from the gift of the power to choose
Immature choosing and the unthinking misstep
Evil consciously embraced and willfully endorsed
130.b13.p: At Caesarea the travelers were delayed because one of the ship’s huge steering paddles was in danger of cracking, and Jesus volunteered to help make a new one. At their inn he met a Taoist merchant from Mongolia who never forgot his words about “⟦Q 130:2.2⟧the living of the heavenly life while on earth by means of daily submission to the will of the heavenly Father.⟦/Q⟧” Back home the merchant taught the one God to his neighbors. The paper regrets that the early church sent no one like Peter to China or like Paul to India.
130.b14.p: A young Greek named Anaxand, who worked beside Jesus on the paddle, asked why the gods, if they cared about him, did not remove his cruel foreman. Jesus surprised him: perhaps you are the salt meant to lead this man into a better way. Why not master his evil by the power of goodness? That night Anaxand and the foreman came together to seek Jesus’ advice, and both later became believers.
130.b15.p: When Ganid asked why he spent so much time visiting strangers, Jesus replied that no man is a stranger to one who knows God, and that knowing and loving one’s brothers and sisters is the supreme experience of living. Asked whether a dog has a soul, Jesus explained that a dog can know its master but cannot know God, who is spirit, and so it cannot have a spiritual experience. From that day Ganid gave up his belief that human souls pass into the bodies of animals.
130.b16.t: The way of God — partnership with the choice of God
The way of man — deliberate choice based on intelligent reflection
Derived from nature and augmented by training; not reflective, not spiritual
130.b17.q: ⟦Q 130:2.10⟧Will is that manifestation of the human mind which enables the subjective consciousness to express itself objectively and to experience the phenomenon of aspiring to be Godlike.⟦/Q⟧
130.b19.p: When Ganid was thrilled by the great lighthouse of Pharos, Jesus told him that when he returned to India he would be like that lighthouse — a light of life to those who sit in darkness, showing the way to the harbor of salvation. Ganid squeezed his hand and said, “I will.” In the great library, with nearly a million manuscripts, the two discussed all the religions of the world. Jesus pointed out the truth in each, but always added that the religion of the Jews had come to the clearest recognition of the Universal Father.
130.b20.p: Under Jesus’ direction Ganid gathered the teachings of the world religions that recognized a Universal Deity, and he was surprised to find that the best authors all more or less recognized an eternal God. After hearing the lectures in the museum, Ganid urged Jesus to stand up and teach the professors, but Jesus smiled and declined. He impressed on the boy that philosophies are religions only in the sense that they lead men to find God.
130.b21.q: ⟦Q 130:3.7⟧The true teacher maintains his intellectual integrity by ever remaining a learner.⟦/Q⟧
130.b23.p: On the night before they left Alexandria, after meeting a professor who lectured on Plato, Jesus gave Ganid a long talk on the nature of reality. The source of universe reality is the Infinite, and everything except the Absolutes may change. Only in perfection, harmony, and unanimity of will can the creature become one with the Creator. Just as a one-eyed person cannot see depth, neither the material scientist alone nor the spiritual mystic alone can grasp the true depths of reality.
130.b24.t: The endowment that keeps its identity through unlimited change
An adaptation to universe situations — its meaning is adaptability, its value is progressability
Demonstrable; a possession of the mind
Experienced; an experience of the soul, the progressing self
What interprets reality when knowledge and truth are harmonized
The shadow of relative incompleteness, not an actual universe quality
130.b25.p: The next morning Ganid asked more about evil. Jesus explained that evil is a relativity concept: it arises from the imperfections seen in the shadow cast by a finite universe as it obscures the light of the Infinite. He added that all static, dead concepts are potentially evil, and that they invariably hold back science, politics, society, and religion.
130.b27.p: The travelers went to Crete only to rest and climb the mountains, yet even there Jesus and Ganid led many souls to higher levels of thinking and living. On a mountainside Gonod had his first long talk with Jesus about religion, and it was here that he first proposed that Jesus come with them to India. When Ganid asked why he did not become a public teacher, Jesus answered that everything must await the coming of its time — time alone will ripen the green fruit upon the tree.
130.b28.p: At Fair Havens Jesus pulled a slave girl away from a drunken man who was attacking her, and simply held the man off with his outstretched arm until he had worn himself out. This episode made Ganid wish he could change the caste system of India, but he never quite understood why Jesus did not strike the man.
130.b29.h: 6. The Young Man Who Was Afraid
130.b30.p: In the mountains Jesus met a young man weighed down by helplessness and inferiority. When he would not talk, Jesus first asked him the way to Phenix and let him help. Then he turned back and said that he, in turn, knew the way to the city of the young man’s disappointed hopes. “⟦Q 130:6.2⟧But I did not ask you for anything,⟦/Q⟧” the youth stammered. Jesus answered that he had asked — not with words but with longing looks.
130.b31.p: “Arise!” Jesus told him. Small enemies might surround him, but the big things and the real things of the world and the universe were on his side. He had a strong body, a capable mind, and above all the spirit that lived within him. He must refuse to be a slave of fear, be born again, and hasten back to duty. This young man, Fortune, later became the leader of the Christians in Crete. At Cyrene Jesus and Ganid cared for an injured boy named Rufus, whose father, Simon, would one day carry the cross of the stranger who had befriended his son.
130.b32.t: For one who is born again
130.b33.h: 7. At Carthage—Discourse on Time and Space
130.b34.p: On the way to Carthage Gonod and Ganid discovered that Jesus was a good storyteller and that he had grown up in Galilee. When Ganid asked how to make friends, Jesus said: become interested in your fellows, learn how to love them, and watch for the chance to do something for them which you are sure they want done.
130.b35.p: At Carthage he talked with a Mithraic priest about time and eternity. Time is the stream of events perceived by creature consciousness, and on the inhabited worlds human personality, indwelt by the Paradise Father’s spirit, is the only physically related reality that can transcend the material sequence of events. As man ascends, what once looked like a line of events will be seen more and more as a related whole, and his ideas of time and space will come ever closer to the timeless and spaceless concepts of the Absolutes.
130.b36.h: 8. On the Way to Naples and Rome
130.b37.p: At Malta Jesus talked with Claudus, a young man who had thought of taking his life. Claudus left resolved to face life like a man. He later preached the gospel with Peter, but he never knew that the man who had inspired him was Jesus himself. At Syracuse Ezra, a backslidden Jew who kept the tavern, despaired that he could not find God. Jesus told him that if he truly wanted to find God, that desire was itself evidence that he had already found him.
130.b38.q: ⟦Q 130:8.2⟧Your trouble is not that you cannot find God, for the Father has already found you⟦/Q⟧
130.b39.p: At Messina Jesus encouraged a boy who sold fruit to learn, after feeding the body, how also to feed the soul. At Naples he and Ganid spread good cheer with many smiles upon hundreds of men, women, and children. Then they went on by way of Capua and along the Appian Way toward Rome, the greatest city in all the world.
130.b41.p: Paper 130 is made not of public sermons but of meetings along the road. Jesus protected the motive of a young man who held to the story of Jonah. He told a worker who resented his cruel foreman to master evil with good. He told a frightened young man to be born again and go back to his duty. He never put his own name forward, yet these brief encounters later bore the fruit of faith in many places. His own words run through the whole journey: to one who knows God, no one is a stranger.
130.b42.t: Do not run from duty; evil comes from wrong choosing
Master evil with good, and meet the stranger as a brother
The true teacher always remains a learner
When knowledge and truth are harmonized, the world of reality appears
Everything must await the coming of its time
6. The Young Man Who Was Afraid
Do not be a slave of fear; be born again and return to duty
7. At Carthage—Discourse on Time and Space
Spirit-indwelt personality can transcend the sequence of time
8. On the Way to Naples and Rome
The desire to find God shows that he has already found you
130.b44.box: Because no one is a stranger to one who knows God, Jesus loved each person he met on the road as a brother and gave each one the truth.
131.title: The World’s Religions
131.b0.ask: “How did Ganid find the same traces of the one God in the religions of lands so far apart?”
131.b2.p: In Paper 130 Jesus met many people on the road to Rome in the company of Ganid and Gonod. Paper 131 goes back to their stay in Alexandria and shows us the record of the world’s religions that the young man from India gathered there. Ganid employed more than threescore learned translators to collect what the religions of the world taught about God and his relations with mortal man.
131.b3.p: The paper makes one fact plain from the start. All these teachings that portray one God were largely derived, directly or indirectly, from the preaching of the missionaries of Machiventa Melchizedek, who went out from Salem to carry the doctrine of the Most High to the ends of the earth. Ganid arranged his material under ten heads at Alexandria and Rome, and his manuscript was preserved in India for hundreds of years after his death.
131.b4.p: How do religions from lands so far apart, from the Cynics to Confucianism, bear witness to the same one God — and which religion did Ganid finally come to call “our religion”?
131.b5.q: ⟦Q 131:10.2⟧Though we cannot see God, we can know him.⟦/Q⟧
131.b8.p: The ten heads of Ganid’s collection are all branches of a single tree, because the Melchizedek missionaries from Salem set out to spread the doctrine of one God, the Most High, everywhere. Apart from what survived in the Jewish religion, the teachings of Melchizedek’s disciples were best preserved in the doctrines of the Cynics.
131.b9.t: Best preserved outside the Jewish religion
Salvaged by the Kenites, preserved and modified by the Jews
Influenced by Melchizedek missionaries in India up to Buddha’s time
Embodied, with older ideas, in its later teachings
Its founder was in direct contact with the missionaries’ descendants
A third group in India that kept the doctrine of one God
A Far-Eastern faith holding remnants of the early teaching
The Chinese religion holding most of the monotheistic truth
The least God-recognizing, yet it acknowledged one God
The faith Ganid reached through Jesus’ teaching
131.b10.p: The Cynic records picture God as the Most High of heaven and earth, devoid of all anger and enmity, immortal and infinite. Yet he is not far away. God fills all places, and we search for the Most High and then find him in our hearts. The one who knows God looks upon all men as equal, and rich and poor alike are brothers.
131.b12.p: The Kenites of Palestine salvaged much of Melchizedek’s teaching, and from these records, as preserved and modified by the Jews, Jesus and Ganid chose their selections. In them we meet the one God who made heaven and earth, the merciful God who heals the brokenhearted, and the God who leads his people like a shepherd.
131.b13.p: Ganid’s excerpts tie the love of God and the love of neighbor into one cord: love your neighbor as yourself, and whatever you hate, do to no man. Then they list the commandments God has given.
131.b14.t: You shall love me with all your heart
You shall have no gods before me
You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery
You shall not take my name in vain
You shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness
Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy
131.b15.p: This section ends with God’s promise to all who love him supremely and their neighbors as themselves: has he not called them to become like him and to dwell forever with him in Paradise?
131.b17.p: Ganid was shocked to discover how near Buddhism came to being a great and beautiful religion without a personal and universal God. Still, he found records of earlier beliefs that reflected the work of Melchizedek missionaries in India even to the times of Buddha. These records speak of the faith of the Immortal, the faith that creates modesty, uprightness, wisdom, courage, knowledge, and perseverance.
131.b18.t: Man’s true wealth, the endowment of virtue and glory
The fruit of wrongly directed thinking
Every act shall receive its reward
The one who overcomes and subdues himself
131.b19.p: The Buddhist records teach that honest efforts to make amends for past sins give strength to resist future tendencies toward them. They say: pay good for evil; overcome evil with the good. And they promise that whoever thinks righteously, speaks nobly, and acts unselfishly will continue to enjoy the delights of heaven after the dissolution of the body.
131.b21.p: The Melchizedek missionaries carried the teaching of one God wherever they went, and much of it, along with older ideas, became part of the later teachings of Hinduism. In these records God is one God, alone and by himself, our Maker and the last destiny of the soul. Those who learn to know him become immortal.
131.b22.p: The Hindu records stress again and again that God dwells within us. His primeval spirit dwells within the mortal soul, and the Eternal Witness to vice and virtue lives in man’s heart. Then comes a prayer of India:
131.b23.t: The three petitions of the prayer
Where it asks to be led
131.b24.p: Without God the soul is a prisoner; to know God releases the soul. The records pray to be saved from the threefold ruin of hell — lust, wrath, and avarice — and they say that the God-knowing soul rises in the universe like the cream appears on top of the milk.
131.b26.p: Zoroaster himself was in direct contact with descendants of the early Melchizedek missionaries, and their doctrine of one God became central to the religion he founded in Persia. Apart from Judaism, no religion of that day held more of the Salem teachings. In these records God is the source of all luminosity, who stretches out his beneficent hand to both the righteous and the wicked.
131.b27.p: Zoroastrianism says that God is farthest from us and at the same time nearest to us, for he dwells within our souls. The believer repents of offenses in thought, word, or act, knowing that forgiveness takes away the bonds of sin. And he asks for mercy because he aspires to perfection — because he would be like God.
131.b29.p: The third group in India to preserve Melchizedek’s doctrine of one God were known in those days as the Suduanists; today they are known as followers of Jainism. They taught that those who walk in the paths of righteousness will find a place in heaven, and that the soul of man may ascend to the highest heaven and attain perfection.
131.b30.p: In this teaching man’s invincible foe is the self. The self shows itself in four great passions, and man’s greatest victory is the conquest of himself.
131.b31.t: The four great passions of the self
Treat your fellows as you would like to be treated
131.b33.p: The records of this Far-Eastern religion had only recently reached the library at Alexandria, and Ganid had never heard of it. Yet it too held remnants of the early Melchizedek teaching. Its Lord is the maker of heaven and earth, yet he has regard for the prayer of the poorest man.
131.b34.p: Shinto warns especially against pride. Pride obscures God, and every hair of pride shuts off saving light as if by a great cloud. Prayers are heard when one comes with a clean heart, free from falsehood and hypocrisy, with a soul that reflects truth like a mirror.
131.b36.p: Melchizedek’s messengers went far into China. Of the Chinese religions, the one that lasted longest and held most of the monotheistic truth was Taoism. Its Supreme One existed before the heavens and the earth; he stands alone and changes not; he is the world’s mother, and all creation moves around him.
131.b37.p: Taoism compares true goodness to water: it blesses everything and harms nothing, and it seeks even the lowest places that others avoid. The Supreme fosters and perfects the creature without compelling him; he guides without self-assertion and ministers progression without domination.
131.b38.q: ⟦Q 131:8.5⟧God does not reward man for what he does but for what he is⟦/Q⟧
131.b40.p: Even the least God-recognizing of the world’s great religions acknowledged the one God of the Melchizedek missionaries and their successors. The Confucian records say that what Heaven appoints is without error, that benevolence is Heaven’s choicest gift to men, and that the virtues of man are the fruit of Heaven’s nobility bestowed on his soul.
131.b41.p: These records make faith the ground of life. If any virtue is found in me, it is the manifestation of Heaven who abides with me — and I do not see how a man can live without this good faith. While all creatures die, the spirit of the noble man ascends to the glorious light of final brightness.
131.b43.p: After the hard labor of compiling the teachings of the world’s religions, Ganid set down a summary of the belief he had reached through Jesus’ teaching. He liked to call it “our religion.” It begins with the one Lord, whom we should love with all our mind and heart while loving all his children as we love ourselves.
131.b44.p: Almost every one of the ten records Ganid gathered contained the same rule: treat others as you would be treated. The form varies a little from one to another, but the root is the same.
131.b45.t: The golden rule in its words
The evil you would not have done you, do not to others
Whatsoever you hate do to no man
Do not to others those things you would not wish done to you
Let no man do to another what would be repugnant to himself
Treat your fellow creatures as you would like to be treated
What you do not like when done to yourself, do not to others
Whatsoever I would that men should do to me, that I will do to my fellows
131.b46.p: Ganid’s confession goes one step further. He is no longer satisfied to believe that God is the Father of all his people; from now on he will believe that God is also his own Father. It sometimes frightens him to think that all men are his brothers, but he sees that he cannot rejoice in the fatherhood of God while refusing to accept the brotherhood of man. He sees God in the other religions too, but in “our religion” he finds him more beautiful, loving, merciful, and personal.
131.b47.q: ⟦Q 131:10.8⟧At last I have a religion with a God, a marvelous God, and he is a God of eternal salvation.⟦/Q⟧
131.b49.p: Paper 131 looks like a catalog of world religions, but a single story runs beneath it. The seed of the one God, sown by the Melchizedek missionaries who went out from Salem, grew in different forms in Palestine and India, in Persia, China, and the Far East. As Ganid gathered these traces one by one, he saw two witnesses alive everywhere: that God is far above us yet dwells within our hearts, and that we should treat others as we would be treated. At the end of his long search he arrived at the simplest truth he had learned from Jesus: God is my Father, and therefore every man is my brother.
131.b50.t: Where Melchizedek’s seed was best kept; God is found in the heart
Love of God and love of neighbor are bound together in the commandments
Faith is man’s true wealth, and good overcomes evil
To know God releases the soul from captivity
The God who is farthest is nearest, within the soul
Man’s greatest victory is the conquest of himself
Every hair of pride shuts off saving light
True goodness, like water, seeks the lowest place and never compels
Man’s virtues are the fruit of Heaven’s nobility
If God is my Father, every man is my brother
131.b52.box: The traces of the one God scattered through all religions come together in a single truth: God is my Father, and all men are my brothers.
132.title: The Sojourn at Rome
132.b0.ask: “In Rome, the capital of the world, how did Jesus prepare the way for the gospel without ever attacking error — by truth alone?”
132.b2.p: In Paper 131 Ganid gathered the records of the world’s religions at Alexandria. Paper 132 shows the six months the travelers spent in Rome. On the third day after their arrival the three of them appeared before the emperor Tiberius. When they had gone, the emperor remarked of Jesus that if he had that fellow’s kingly bearing and gracious manner, he would be a real emperor. The chief reason Jesus agreed to this journey was his desire to study and mingle with mortals gathered from every part of the world.
132.b3.p: The most valuable experience of the stay in Rome was Jesus’ contact with the city’s religious leaders. He chose five of the leading Stoics, eleven of the Cynics, and sixteen leaders of the mystery cults — thirty-two in all — and spent much of his spare time with them. Never once did he attack their errors. Instead he picked out the truth in what they taught and so illuminated it that the truth soon crowded out the error. Thirty of them later became pivotal figures in establishing Christianity in Rome, yet none of them ever realized who the scribe of Damascus had been.
132.b4.p: What, then, did Jesus give to each person he met in this city — the philosopher and the priest, the senator and the slaveholder, the lost child and the widow?
132.b5.q: ⟦Q 132:3.2⟧Truth cannot be defined with words, only by living.⟦/Q⟧
132.b8.p: The authors of this paper tell us that, looking back over nineteen centuries, they see three factors of paramount value in preparing for the rapid spread of Christianity through Europe. The third of these was the early preparation of these thirty Romans.
132.b9.t: Three factors in the spread of Christianity
His choosing and holding as an apostle
His death led to the winning of Saul of Tarsus
Their preparation for later leadership of the new religion
132.b10.p: Early in his stay Jesus talked all night with Angamon, leader of the Stoics. He taught that the standard of true values must be sought in the spiritual world and on divine levels of eternal reality; all lower and material standards are transient and partial. The scientist as such is limited to discovering the relations of material facts. When he claims to be a materialist or an idealist, he has already stepped into philosophy.
132.b11.p: Unless moral insight and spiritual attainment grow along with it, the unlimited advance of a purely materialistic culture may in the end become a menace to civilization. Scientists and religionists alike stand on trial before the bar of human need. Instead of warring with each other, they must justify their existence by serving human progress.
132.b13.p: Mardus, the leader of the Cynics in Rome, asked Jesus about good and evil. Jesus answered that good and evil are words for relative levels of human understanding of the universe. The morally lazy may take current social customs or religious traditions as their standard of good. But the soul that is to survive into eternity must make a living, personal choice by the standards of the divine spirit that the Father has sent to dwell in the heart of man.
132.b15.p: An experience is good when it heightens the appreciation of beauty, strengthens the moral will, and enlarges the capacity to love and serve one’s fellows. Until we reach Paradise, goodness will always be more of a quest than a possession. And while the possibility of evil is necessary to moral choosing, actual evil need not be experienced at all.
132.b16.q: ⟦Q 132:2.10⟧Evil becomes a reality of personal experience only when a moral mind makes evil its choice.⟦/Q⟧
132.b18.p: Nabon, high priest of the Mithraic cult, actually hoped to make a convert of Jesus. He little realized that Jesus was preparing him to become one of the early converts to the gospel of the kingdom. Jesus taught him that truth is always more than knowledge.
132.b19.t: The religious experience of spiritual living
132.b20.p: Because man is mentally lazy and terribly afraid of the unknown, he tends to crystallize science, formulate philosophy, and dogmatize truth. Yet truth can never become his without faith, for his thoughts and ideals will never rise higher than his faith, his sublime hope. Plants and animals survive by passing identical particles of themselves to the next generation; the human soul survives death by identity with the immortal spark of divinity that dwells within it.
132.b21.p: Spiritual evolution is the experience of choosing goodness more and more freely, while the possibility of evil steadily shrinks. The attainment of perfect spiritual self-restraint is the same as complete freedom and personal liberty.
132.b23.p: In Rome Jesus came to know people of every race and class. In each meeting he had a double purpose: to learn how they were reacting to life, and to say or do something to make that life richer. He usually drew people out by asking questions, and to those he taught the most, he said the least. Those who gained most were the overburdened and anxious, who found in him a sympathetic listener. In this way he came into affectionate and uplifting contact with more than five hundred people.
132.b24.t: Spent his life urging that the people should support the government, not the reverse
Freed one hundred and seventeen slaves the next day
Learned that his patients had minds and souls as well as bodies
A Roman soldier by the Tiber
Be brave of heart as well as of hand
Marcus, the speaker at the forum
Later became Peter’s successor and kept preaching the gospel
Jesus spoke for him; the case was reopened and he was freed
132.b25.p: Speaking for the poor man, Jesus said that justice makes a nation great. Woe to any nation where only those with money and influence can secure ready justice. Civil government is founded on justice, even as true religion is founded on mercy. Of all his personal ministry in those days, this came nearest to a public appearance.
132.b27.p: A wealthy Stoic citizen, introduced by Angamon, asked whether he should keep his wealth or give it away. Jesus made it clear that his advice was for this one man only, not for other rich men, and urged him first to ask honestly where his wealth had come from. He then named ten ways of gaining wealth and gave his counsel for each.
132.b28.t: Pass the legitimate part on; use the unfair part for justice and restitution
Take a reward, but provide for many to share it
Take only the profit you would gladly allow a fellow trader
Restore it to those robbed, or to their children
First cleanse your capital, and never take usury
Do not claim an unfair portion of the rewards
Treat it as a trust for the good of your group
Make haste to restore it in full to its owners
Never jeopardize the trust; take only what honest men would allow
Truly your own, so long as it harms no one
132.b29.p: When in honest doubt, Jesus said, let your decisions favor those in need and those who suffer undeserved hardship; God would not condemn you for erring on the side of mercy. The rich man promised to begin managing all his wealth by this counsel the very next day.
132.b31.p: In Rome the Creator of a universe spent several hours restoring a lost, crying boy to his mother. Jesus told Ganid that most people are like that lost child: they spend much of their time crying in fear and sorrow when they are only a short distance from safety. Those who know God should count it a privilege, not a duty, to guide their fellows. From that day on, for the rest of his life, Ganid was always on the lookout for lost children.
132.b32.p: The two visited again and again a widow with five children whose husband had been killed in an accident. They provided food and clothing and found work for the eldest boy. When Gonod laughed that Jesus was making his son into a philosopher or a philanthropist, Jesus smiled and said perhaps they would make him all four, so that he could hear four tones of life’s melody instead of one. When Gonod urged him to write a book, Jesus answered: not a book — his mission was to live a life in this generation and for all generations.
132.b34.p: On the way to the northern Italian lakes they met a thoughtless pagan, and Jesus did not draw him into conversation. The man was not hungry for truth. You cannot reveal God to those who do not seek for him, Jesus explained; if we know God, our real business on earth is so to live that the Father can reveal himself in our lives.
132.b35.p: In the mountains of Switzerland Gonod asked directly about Buddha. Jesus answered that Buddha was a great man, even a prophet, but an orphan prophet — he early lost sight of his spiritual Father. He guided his ship of salvation right up to the harbor, and there, because of faulty charts, it ran aground.
132.b36.t: Failed clearly to discover him in mind
Largely failed to know him in spirit
132.b37.p: When Ganid proposed that he and his teacher make a new religion together, Jesus answered that religions are not made; they grow up over long periods, while the revelations of God flash upon earth in the lives of men who reveal God to their fellows. Ganid did not know it, but they were making a new and everlasting religion right then and there — the revelation of God to man through, and in, Jesus.
132.b38.q: ⟦Q 132:7.9⟧When man goes in partnership with God, great things may, and do, happen.⟦/Q⟧
132.b40.p: Paper 132 shows the six months Jesus spent in the capital of the world. To philosophers he gave true values and truth; to a priest, faith; to a rich man, the way of stewardship; to a poor man, justice; to a lost child, the way home. He never attacked error anywhere. He lit up the truth people already held and let that truth push the error out by itself. The thirty minds prepared in this way later became fertile ground for the gospel. And his talk with Ganid gathers the meaning of it all into one sentence: religion is not made; it grows in lives that reveal God.
132.b41.t: The standard of value lies in eternal reality; science and religion must serve human need
Evil becomes real only when a moral mind chooses it
Knowledge deals with facts, wisdom with relationships, truth with reality values
He led by questions and listening, and lifted more than five hundred people
Examine the sources of wealth, and in doubt favor those in need
Guiding our fellows is a privilege, not a duty
Religions are not made; God is revealed in lives that show him
132.b43.box: Jesus never attacked error; he lit up the truth in people — and God is revealed through the lives that show him.
133.title: The Return from Rome
133.b0.ask: “On the road home from Rome, what did Jesus teach about mercy and justice, the soul and the mind — and how did he part from Ganid?”
133.b2.p: In Paper 132 Jesus spent six months in Rome among religious leaders and hundreds of ordinary people. Paper 133 follows the journey back, from Rome until he parted from Ganid and his father in Mesopotamia. Jesus left Rome without saying good-bye to any of his friends. The Stoics, Cynics, and mystery cultists who had known him kept meeting in small groups, remembering his teachings, until the first Christian preachers arrived.
133.b3.p: The travelers walked leisurely across Italy along the Appian Way toward Tarentum, meeting all sorts of people. On the way Ganid asked what Jesus thought of India’s caste system. Jesus answered that although people differ in many ways, before God all mortals stand on an equal footing. In God’s eyes there are only two groups: those who desire to do his will and those who do not.
133.b4.p: As they passed through Corinth and Athens, Ephesus and Cyprus, Antioch and Ur, what did Jesus teach about mercy and justice, and about science, the soul, and the mind?
133.b5.q: ⟦Q 133:0.3⟧God is truly no respecter of persons.⟦/Q⟧
133.b8.p: Near Tarentum they saw a bullying youth brutally attacking a smaller boy. Jesus rescued the little one and held the bully until the smaller boy had escaped. But the moment Jesus let him go, Ganid began to thrash the bully — and Jesus promptly stopped him. Ganid protested: if mercy requires rescuing the small boy, does not justice demand punishing the offender?
133.b9.t: Always the work of the individual
The function of social, governmental, or universe groups
133.b10.p: Jesus explained that no two people are likely to agree on what punishment would satisfy justice, so the administration of justice rests with the group, its chosen representatives, or those who fully know all the circumstances. Asked what he would do if someone attacked him, he said that against a creature without moral judgment he would defend himself fully; but he would not punish a fellow man in advance and without judgment. He would try by every means to prevent and dissuade him. He was absolutely assured that the entire universe was friendly to him. On another occasion he said that organized society has every right to use force in carrying out its just mandates.
133.b12.p: At the ship landing a man was mistreating his wife. Jesus tapped him gently on the shoulder and asked to speak with him in private. What terrible thing had happened, he asked, to lead such a strong man to attack the mother of his children before all eyes? It was not so much his words as his kindly look and sympathetic smile that touched the man’s heart, and he was sorry for his lack of self-control.
133.b13.p: Jesus told him that man has no rightful authority over woman unless she has willingly given it. Men and women are partners with God, for together they create beings who may possess immortal souls. A man should love and cherish his wife as the Father in heaven honors and exalts the Infinite Spirit. Hearing this, Gonod resolved to reorganize his own home when he returned to India.
133.b14.q: ⟦Q 133:2.2⟧The loving care and consideration which a man is willing to bestow upon his wife and their children are the measure of that man's attainment of the higher levels of creative and spiritual self-consciousness.⟦/Q⟧
133.b16.p: At Corinth Ganid became very interested in the Jewish religion and loved to observe the family life of Crispus, chief ruler of the synagogue. Meanwhile Jesus held more than twenty sessions with Crispus, teaching him better ways of religious living. Years later, when Paul was driven from that synagogue, Crispus and his whole family embraced the new religion. Aquila, one of the Cynics Jesus had met in Rome, also helped Paul there together with Priscilla.
133.b17.p: One evening two public women approached them, and Ganid sharply waved them away. Jesus said: who are we that we should sit in judgment on these women? They were not willfully wicked; in discouragement bordering on despair they had given in to the pressure of the hour. Ganid apologized, and Jesus took the women to the home of Justus, asking his wife Martha to help them begin a new life. The elder woman died soon after with bright hopes of eternal survival, and the younger became a lifelong member of the first Christian church in Corinth.
133.b19.p: Of the many people Jesus and Ganid talked with during their two months in Corinth, more than half later became members of the Christian community. Jesus spoke to each according to his work and situation.
133.b20.t: Grind the grains of truth in the mill of living experience so that even the weak can receive them
Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s
The mystery of eternal salvation dwells within your own soul
The great thing in all human experience is knowing the God whose spirit lives within you
While you build the mansions of time for others, secure your title to the mansions of eternity
Judge justly, even mercifully, as you would be judged
Show hospitality as one who entertains the children of the Most High
We shall meet again in the worlds of light
Every honest attempt to communicate with the indwelling spirit meets with certain success
There are two things you cannot run away from — God and yourself
Appeal for forgiveness to the Judge who sees your real motives
133.b22.p: At their inn in Athens a Greek philosopher lectured on science for almost three hours. Then Jesus spoke. Scientists may someday measure gravitation, light, and electricity, he said, but they can never scientifically tell us what these things are.
133.b23.t: The wisdom that correlates quantitative and qualitative observations
133.b24.p: Logic and mathematics are reliable in the material world but not wholly dependable in the problems of life. If one man can shear a sheep in ten minutes, ten men cannot shear it in one; they would get in one another’s way. On the other hand, a group of people working in harmony stands for a force far greater than the simple sum of its parts. The mind can grasp the unity of the universe only by seeing that quantitative fact and qualitative value have a common cause in the Paradise Father — and the real universe is friendly to every child of the eternal God.
133.b26.p: At Ephesus Ganid bought a little silver shrine from the temple of Artemis, and that night they talked at length about the worship of things made with human hands. Later a progressive thinker of the local school of philosophy asked Jesus what he meant by the word “soul,” which he used so often. Jesus explained:
133.b27.t: The self-reflective, truth-discerning, and spirit-perceiving part of man
The divine spirit arrives with the mind’s first moral activity, and the soul is born
The spiritualization of the self-realization of the moral consciousness, giving it survival value
Lack of harmony between moral and purely intellectual self-consciousness
133.b28.p: A stagnant soul is a dying soul. Neither material science nor pure spirit-testing can demonstrate the soul’s existence, yet every morally conscious mortal knows of his own soul as a real and actual personal experience.
133.b29.h: 7. The Sojourn at Cyprus—Discourse on Mind
133.b30.p: While they were resting in the mountains of Cyprus, Ganid suddenly fell gravely ill with a raging fever. Far from any village, Jesus nursed him skillfully and tenderly, and Gonod was amazed at his gentleness. After Ganid recovered, he asked what it means that man has a higher form of self-consciousness than the animals. Jesus stressed that self-consciousness is a reality: when any animal becomes self-conscious, it becomes a primitive man.
133.b31.p: Ideas are not simply a record of sensations; they are sensations plus the reflective interpretation of the personal self, and the self is more than the sum of its sensations. People differ so greatly in their lives not only because of heredity and environment, but also because of how far each self has become unified with the indwelling spirit of the Father.
133.b32.q: ⟦Q 133:7.12⟧The supremely happy and efficiently unified mind is the one wholly dedicated to the doing of the will of the Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧
133.b33.p: The human mind does not well stand the strain of trying to serve both good and evil. True peace does not come from surrendering noble aspirations or compromising spiritual ideals, but from the stalwart assertion of the triumph of what is true — by overcoming evil with the potent force of good.
133.b35.p: Antioch was the third city of the empire in size and the first in wickedness. Jesus would not go with the others to the grove of Daphne, and as they drew nearer to Palestine he grew sober and reflective. When Ganid asked why he showed so little interest in the city, he said only that perhaps he would come back there sometime.
133.b36.p: Here Ganid put Jesus’ teachings into practice. An Indian employee of his father’s had become so disgruntled that his dismissal was being considered. Ganid talked with him at length about the Father in heaven, and what helped most was a Hebrew proverb he quoted: “⟦Q 133:8.3⟧Whatsoever your hand finds to do, do that with all your might.⟦/Q⟧”
133.b38.p: On the caravan trip across the desert, when Jesus helped load their twenty camels and offered to drive their own, Ganid exclaimed, “⟦Q 133:9.1⟧Teacher, is there anything that you cannot do?⟦/Q⟧” At Ur, the birthplace of Abraham, the two talked long about the difference between knowledge, wisdom, and truth.
133.b39.p: At last, at Charax, the day of parting came. Ganid said he loved his teacher, for he thought the Father in heaven must be something like him — and that, more than the teaching, he would never forget Jesus himself. Gonod bade farewell to a great teacher who had made them better and helped them to know God. They never learned that Jesus of Nazareth was their own Joshua the teacher. Ganid grew up to be a worthy successor to his father in India and spread abroad many of the truths he had learned. So ended the chapter that might be called the mission of Joshua the teacher.
133.b41.p: Paper 133 is the story of the cities Jesus passed through on his way home from Rome, but even more it is the story of the people he met there. He broke up a fight and showed where mercy ends and justice begins. He taught a husband who struck his wife what a husband’s true authority is, gave two despairing women the chance of a new life, and gave the miller, the judge, and the condemned man each a truth to hold in his own place. In Athens, Ephesus, and Cyprus he explained science, the soul, and the mind, showing that fact and value are unified in the one Father. And as Ganid’s farewell reminds us, what lasted longest was not the teaching but the teacher himself, who was so much like the Father in heaven.
133.b42.t: Section
Key message
1. Mercy and Justice
Mercy is the work of the individual; punishment belongs to the group
2. Embarking at Tarentum
To love and honor one’s wife is Godlike
3. At Corinth
Who are we to judge those who have given way to despair?
4. Personal Work in Corinth
He gave each person the truth that fit his work and life
5. At Athens—Discourse on Science
Fact and value find their common cause in the Paradise Father
6. At Ephesus—Discourse on the Soul
The soul is born on moral self-consciousness and is known by experience
7. The Sojourn at Cyprus—Discourse on Mind
The most unified mind is wholly dedicated to the Father’s will
8. At Antioch
Whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might
9. In Mesopotamia
Ganid never forgot the teacher, even more than the teaching
133.b44.box: God is no respecter of persons, and Jesus left with each person he met the very truth that person needed.
134.title: The Transition Years
134.b0.ask: “How did Jesus, still living as a private man, win the sovereignty of his universe and come to stand at the door of his public mission?”
134.b2.p: In Paper 133 Jesus parted from Ganid and his father, closing the chapter of Joshua the teacher. Paper 134 covers the roughly two years between that parting and his baptism — the transition from private life to public career. Having carefully studied the peoples and lands of the Mediterranean, Jesus now made his final decision about the rest of his life on earth. He fully approved the plan that he be born of Jewish parents in Palestine, and of his own free will he returned to Galilee to wait for the beginning of his lifework as a public teacher of truth.
134.b3.p: He decided to finish his mortal career in the same land in which he had entered human experience as a helpless babe. His Urantia career began among the Jews in Palestine, and he chose to end it in Palestine and among the Jews.
134.b4.p: Where did Jesus go during this time of waiting, what did he teach, and what did he accomplish in the solitude of Mount Hermon?
134.b5.q: ⟦Q 134:8.8⟧The will of my Father in Paradise be done.⟦/Q⟧
134.b8.p: After leaving Ganid and Gonod at Charax, Jesus returned by way of Babylon and Damascus to Nazareth. Passing through Capernaum, he turned over to his brother James the little house that John Zebedee had bought for him. His family believed he had spent his time away studying in Alexandria, and Jesus neither confirmed nor denied it.
134.b9.p: Simon and Jude had put off their weddings because they wanted their eldest brother’s blessing, and in early March of this year they were married at a double wedding. Now only Ruth, the youngest, was left at home with Mary. When the conductor of a large caravan fell ill, Jesus volunteered to take his place for a year. Mary and Ruth moved to the house in Capernaum, where they lived for the rest of Mary’s life.
134.b10.q: ⟦Q 134:1.7⟧These were the in-between times, the transition stage of that being who began life as God appearing as man, and who was now making ready to complete his earth career as man appearing as God.⟦/Q⟧
134.b11.h: 2. The Caravan Trip to the Caspian
134.b12.p: On April 1, A.D. 24, Jesus joined the caravan as its conductor. It went from Jerusalem by way of Damascus and Lake Urmia, through Assyria, Media, and Parthia, to the southeastern Caspian Sea region, and a full year passed before he returned. He was responsible for the goods in his charge and for the safety of the travelers, and he carried out these duties faithfully, efficiently, and wisely.
134.b13.p: This trip took Jesus nearer to the Orient than any other. He made intimate contact with every surviving race of Urantia except the red man, and Europeans from the far West and Asians from the far East alike listened to his words. The vast majority of those who talked with him were made better for the rest of their lives. When he returned to Capernaum on April 1, A.D. 25, he never again lived with his family.
134.b15.p: On an island near the city of Urmia stood a lecture amphitheater dedicated to “⟦Q 134:3.1|99:1.6|103:6.7⟧the spirit of religion⟦/Q⟧” — really a temple of the philosophy of religions. It had been built by a wealthy merchant named Cymboyton and his three sons, and its founder lived and died without ever revealing his own religious beliefs. Every teacher had to represent a religion that recognized some sort of supreme Deity, and any teacher who showed intolerance or a contentious spirit was promptly dismissed.
134.b16.t: More than thirty religions and religious cults
About seventy-five teachers, five of them independent
An independent teacher representing no organized religion
Twenty-four lectures on “⟦Q 134:3.4|134:3.5|134:4.1⟧The Brotherhood of Men⟦/Q⟧”
Twelve sessions of questions, discussion, and debate
134.b17.p: These were the most systematic and formal of all the Master’s teachings on Urantia. But conditions in the twentieth century are so different from those of Jesus’ day that the next two sections are not a record of his words. Three secondary midwayers, appointed by the Melchizedek chairman of the revelatory commission, restated his teaching as it applies to the present-day world.
134.b19.p: The brotherhood of men is founded on the fatherhood of God. The kingdom of heaven is neither material nor merely intellectual; it is a spiritual relationship between God and man. As long as different religions recognize the spirit sovereignty of God the Father, they will remain at peace. Only when one religion claims to be superior and to hold exclusive authority over the others does it become intolerant and begin to persecute.
134.b20.t: The temptation to seek power over one another
Spiritually, a sovereign God; socially, Cymboyton
134.b21.p: Because God gives a fragment of his spirit to dwell in every human heart, all people are spiritually equal. There can be no lasting religious peace until all religious groups freely give up their notions of divine favor, chosen people, and religious sovereignty.
134.b22.q: ⟦Q 134:4.7⟧Spiritually, all men are equal. The kingdom of heaven is free from castes, classes, social levels, and economic groups. You are all brethren.⟦/Q⟧
134.b24.p: The midwayers say plainly that in this section they have departed more widely from the substance of the Urmia lectures, in order to show what they mean for the critical stage of the twentieth century. War will never end so long as nations cling to the illusion of unlimited national sovereignty. On an inhabited world there are only two levels of relative sovereignty: the spiritual free will of the individual and the collective sovereignty of mankind as a whole.
134.b25.t: Parental power, the first organization of political power
Families overlap into clans of blood kin
Clans unite into larger political groupings
Trade, commerce, and conquest unify the tribes
The final consummation of political growth
134.b26.p: As sovereignty passes to larger groups, minor wars decrease, but the potential for greater wars grows. The loyalty that made one stage possible hinders the next, so patriotism complicates the way to a government of all mankind. A league of nations can prevent small wars but not world wars among the great powers. Just as the forty-eight American states stopped fighting each other once they gave up their sovereignty to the federal government, the nations will begin to enjoy peace when they surrender their sovereignty to a global government. Citizens are not born for the benefit of governments; governments are created for the benefit of men.
134.b28.p: If one man is to be absolutely free, another must become an absolute slave. Freedom is therefore relative; it is the gift of civilization made possible by the enforcement of law. Religion makes the brotherhood of men spiritually possible, but a government of mankind is needed to deal with its social, economic, and political problems.
134.b29.p: This is not a question of armaments or disarmament. Take away every weapon, and nations will still fight with fists, stones, and clubs as long as they hold to the delusion of national sovereignty. War is not the disease but a symptom; the real disease is the virus of national sovereignty. Under world government the individual would enjoy far more liberty.
134.b31.p: After Cymboyton died, the school at Urmia was troubled. The Christian teachers sent by Abner tried to make their own religion dominant over the other beliefs, never suspecting that the lectures of the caravan conductor had been given by Jesus himself. After five years the school closed.
134.b33.p: Returning from the Caspian, Jesus knew that his world travels were nearly over. This was the year of his solitary wanderings through Palestine and Syria, and in different places he was known by different names. In Antioch he lived for more than two months and worked for three weeks as a tentmaker. Ten years later, when Paul heard his followers there speak of the doctrines of the Damascus scribe, he little knew they had heard the Master himself.
134.b35.p: Then Jesus made his final tour as a private individual through the heart of Palestine, from Beersheba in the south to Dan in the north. In Bethlehem he saw his birthplace. Then his indwelling Thought Adjuster led him away from the dwelling places of men to Mount Hermon, and there he lived alone with God for six weeks.
134.b37.p: In mid-August of A.D. 25 Jesus arranged for a lad named Tiglath to bring him food, and he went up the mountain. He asked his Father to send the guardian seraphim back to be with Tiglath, and he entered the great test with only his indwelling Adjuster to guide him. The superhuman beings he faced on the mountain were real — his archenemies in the system of Satania — not phantoms of a starving mind.
134.b38.p: During these weeks he finished the mortal task of achieving the circles of mind-understanding and personality-control. In the last week came the great temptation, when Satan and Caligastia appeared before him. It had nothing to do with food or temple pinnacles; it concerned the sovereignty of a mighty and glorious universe. To every compromise Lucifer’s emissaries proposed, Jesus gave only one answer: that the will of his Father in Paradise be done.
134.b39.q: ⟦Q 134:8.9⟧On an afternoon in late summer, amid the trees and in the silence of nature, Michael of Nebadon won the unquestioned sovereignty of his universe.⟦/Q⟧
134.b40.p: When Jesus came down from the mountain, the Lucifer rebellion and the Caligastia secession were virtually settled. The universe announcement came months later at his baptism, but the real achievement took place that day on the mountain — so the so-called great temptation came before his baptism, not after it. On the way down Jesus met Tiglath and said only that the period of rest was over and he must return to his Father’s business.
134.b42.p: With John Zebedee, Jesus attended the services of the day of atonement in Jerusalem. To him the ceremony was a travesty on divine justice and infinite mercy, a misrepresentation of his Father’s character, but his Adjuster reminded him that his hour had not yet come. During the feast of tabernacles he withdrew to the hills, telling John that only the watchman must keep vigil while the city sleeps in peace.
134.b43.p: Back in Capernaum, Jesus put on his apron and went to work beside his brother James in the boatshop, saying that it behooved him to keep busy while he waited for his hour to come. He took great pains with the interior finishing of the larger boats, and after this time James never wholly gave up his faith in Jesus’ mission. Reports came of a John who was baptizing in the Jordan and preaching that the kingdom of heaven was at hand. In January of A.D. 26, when John had come up the river near Pella, Jesus laid down his tools and declared, “⟦Q 134:9.8|135:8.3|135:8.5⟧My hour has come.⟦/Q⟧”
134.b45.p: Paper 134 describes the quiet two years in which a private man came to stand at the door of his public mission. Jesus led a caravan to the Caspian and met people of almost every race. At Urmia he left his most systematic teaching: religions live in peace when God alone is their spiritual sovereign. And in the solitude of Mount Hermon, by answering every one of Lucifer’s compromises with nothing but the Father’s will, he won the sovereignty of his universe. Coming down from the mountain, he went back to building boats and waited for his time; when it came, he laid down his tools. The transition ended not in grasping for more, but in complete surrender to the Father’s will.

134.b48.box: By refusing every compromise and choosing only the Father’s will, Jesus won the sovereignty of his universe and came to the hour of his public mission.
